What it says: Paul affirms that the grace of God, that is, his undeserved favor, overflowed to him in abundance. That grace arrived together with the faith and love that are found in Christ Jesus. Paul's wording points to a generous, overflowing kindness that went far beyond anything he had earned.

Context: Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker. He has just recalled that he once blasphemed against Christ and persecuted believers. Even so, God forgave him and placed him in ministry. Paul is not boasting about himself; he wants to show that God's grace was greater than his sin.

For today: If you carry guilt over your past, remember that the grace of Christ is greater than your mistakes. Come before God with sincerity, receive his forgiveness, and let his faith and love transform you and move you to serve others.
exp.4:3:
It says that if a widow has children or grandchildren, they must first learn to show godliness to their own family and repay their parents. Repaying means giving back in return for what was given, returning with care the good they received. Pleasing in the sight of God means that this is something God approves of.

Paul is writing to Timothy, who leads the church in Ephesus, about how to care for widows. Some had no one to support them. Paul teaches that the family should be the first to help, so that the church can truly support the widows who are left completely alone, as the verses that follow show.

Today, showing godliness to our family includes caring for our parents and grandparents as they grow old: visiting them, keeping them company, helping them financially where we can, and not leaving that responsibility to others.
exp.0:10:
This verse says that everything before it about the law and sound teaching agrees with the glorious gospel of God, who is blessed. Paul calls God "blessed," meaning worthy of praise and full of joy in himself. He says that this gospel is the message "with which I have been entrusted," meaning it was placed in his care as a responsibility.

Paul is writing to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He had been speaking about teachers who misused the law and about what goes against sound teaching. Here he says the right standard is the gospel, which Paul received as a treasure to guard and not to change. Right after this, he gives thanks because Christ, though Paul had once been a persecutor, treated him with mercy.

For today: if God entrusts us with his message, we should guard it with humility. We can read the Bible without twisting it and share it faithfully, remembering that everything comes from the grace of God.
exp.3:10:
Paul tells Timothy: "Command and teach these things." The word "command" means to order with authority, and "teach" means to instruct clearly. He is referring to what he has just said: that God is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe, and that because of this hope it is worth working and suffering.

Paul writes this letter to Timothy, a young leader who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Paul wants to encourage him to teach the truths of the gospel firmly, in the face of false teachings. In the next verse he asks him that no one despise his youth, but that he be an example by his life. There are different ways to understand "especially of those who believe," but all of them emphasize that salvation is received through faith.

Teach what the Bible says with firmness, but also with humility and a good example. What you say will carry more weight if your way of living supports it.
exp.1:1:
Paul asks that we pray for kings and for all those who hold authority. Notice that he includes everyone in a position of responsibility, not only those we admire. The reason he gives is so that we may live in peace and quiet, with reverence toward God and good conduct. "Dignity" here describes a respectable and honorable way of living, one that reflects well on the faith we profess.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He gives him instructions about how to live and how to worship. The rulers of that time were not Christians and were sometimes hostile, but Paul still asks that we pray for them. The verses that follow connect this with God's desire that all people be saved.

For today: pray by name for your authorities, even if you do not agree with them. Ask God to guide them with wisdom and justice, and that you may be able to live in peace, respect, and a good testimony.
exp.4:6:
Paul tells Timothy to give these instructions to the believers, so that they will be above reproach. That means Timothy must announce them, command them, and teach them clearly. The purpose is that no one would have grounds to accuse or reproach the people Paul spoke about. "Above reproach" here refers to a fault that others could point out.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who looks after the church in Ephesus. Earlier he spoke about widows who have no one to support them and how they should live. Some think "these things" are the instructions about widows; others think they also include what was said about families. What follows, about caring for one's own, supports both readings.

Today, the church's teachings must be stated clearly and lived out with integrity. If something is important, let us not leave it half-done: let us explain it with love and practice it, so that our lives give no reason for reproach.
exp.5:5:
A life of faith in God, which the Bible calls godliness, brings great gain when it goes together with contentment. Contentment means being at peace and satisfied with what one has.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Earlier he had spoken about false teachers who used religion to make money and caused quarrels. Paul answers them that true gain is not having more, but knowing God and being satisfied. He then adds that we brought nothing into the world and we will take nothing out of it.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are seeking God in order to get something, or whether He himself is our riches. This week, give thanks for the basics you already have, and resist the urge to compare yourself with others.
exp.5:1:
Paul speaks to people who serve as slaves while their masters are also believers. He tells them not to show less respect to their masters just because they now share the same faith and are brothers in Christ. Instead, they should serve them all the more, because those who receive their good service are beloved believers. The phrase about showing disrespect refers to treating someone with contempt. The reference to those receiving good service can be understood in more than one way, and scholars read it in different ways.

Paul writes to Timothy, a young pastor in Ephesus, giving him instructions for the church. In that world slavery was common, and the Christian faith placed slaves and masters on equal footing before God. Paul does not defend the system; rather, he cares for the church's witness, so that no one speaks evil of the name of God.

Today, being brothers in the faith is no excuse for showing less respect or giving less effort. If you work alongside other believers, serve them with more dedication, not less, because your work honors Christ.
exp.1:3:
It says that God wants everyone to be saved and to come to know the truth, that is, the message of the gospel about Jesus Christ. "Everyone" here means people in general. "Wants" expresses his desire and his heart. Christians have understood in different ways how this desire of God relates to his sovereignty and to human freedom, but all agree that it shows his love.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He has just asked for prayer for all people, even for kings and those in authority. The reason is that God, our Savior, wants everyone to be saved, and then he reminds us that Jesus, the one mediator, gave himself for all.

For today: pray for people who are hard for you to love, such as bosses, authorities, or difficult neighbors. If God wants their salvation, you too can ask for it and share the truth with them kindly.
exp.4:1:
It says that Timothy should treat older women with the respect one gives a mother, and younger women with the affection of a brother toward his sisters. The words "older women" and "younger women" refer to women of different ages in the church. "With absolute purity" means with complete cleanness of intention, without any doubtful or flirtatious conduct.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He wants to teach him to treat each group in the congregation as if they were family. That is why this verse follows what he said about older and younger men, and it prepares the topic of widows.

For today: in the church, treat each person as family. With those of the opposite sex, watch your words, your gestures, and your moments alone, so that everything is clean and honors God.
exp.5:12:
Paul gives Timothy a serious charge, as someone speaking with witnesses present. He does so in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus. Jesus made the good confession in his testimony before Pontius Pilate, openly declaring the truth about who he was, with courage.

Paul, now an older man, writes to Timothy, the young leader of the church in Ephesus. He has just asked him to flee the love of money and to pursue righteousness and faith. Now he reminds him that his calling is lived under the gaze of God. He sets Jesus before him as the example of faithfulness, even in the face of a trial that would lead him to the cross.

For today: when it is hard to be faithful at work, at home, or at school, remember that God sees you and that Jesus has already walked that road. Ask him for the courage to speak the truth with love and to stand firm.
exp.4:2:
Paul asks Timothy to honor the widows who are truly widows. "Honor" here means to respect, value, and also help with what they need. "Truly widows" refers to women who have been left alone, with no family to support them.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus, to give him guidance on how to treat different groups of believers. The verses that follow explain that if a widow has children or grandchildren, they should look after her first. The church was to care for those who were truly left without help and who put their trust in God.

For today: think of a widow or an older person who is alone in your church or your family. Call her, visit her, or help her with something concrete, such as a meal or an errand. In this way you show her that her life matters and that God has not forgotten her.
exp.2:0:
It says this is a trustworthy saying: if anyone aspires to be an overseer, he desires a noble task. "Trustworthy saying" means something sure and true. "Aspires" here means to want something eagerly. An "overseer" is someone who watches over and looks after the church; the Greek word speaks of an overseer. Here the verse speaks of a task, not a title of prestige.

Paul writes this letter to Timothy, who served the church in Ephesus. He wants to guide him on how to set the life of the congregation in order. That is why, after encouraging this desire, he immediately lists the character that is expected: blameless, temperate, hospitable, able to teach. Scholars discuss exactly how "overseer" relates to "elder" or "pastor," though they are closely linked.

Today, desiring to serve others in the church is a good thing, but it is wise for that desire to go together with humility and a character that is cared for every day.
exp.4:4:
She says that the true widow is the one who is truly in need and left all alone, with no family to support her. That is why she puts her hope in God and keeps bringing her requests to him in prayer, night and day. Her "petitions" are the earnest, humble requests she brings before God. "Left all alone" describes a woman who has no one to lean on.

Paul writes to Timothy, his co-worker, who was overseeing the church in Ephesus. He gives guidance about whom the church should help. The verses before this one ask that children and grandchildren take care of their widows first. Here he describes the widow with no one, whose life of faith stands in contrast to the one who lives given over to pleasure (v. 6).

For today: we can walk alongside and support those who are alone, starting with our own family. And when we feel alone, we can make prayer a daily refuge, trusting that God hears us.
exp.1:7:
Paul says that he wants the men in every place to pray, lifting up holy hands, that is, with a clean life before God. And that they do so without anger or dissension.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He has just spoken of Christ giving himself for all, so he asks for prayer for all people. Now he teaches how believers should pray. Lifting up the hands was a common posture of prayer at that time. What matters is not the gesture but a clean heart at peace with others.

Before praying, examine your heart. If you hold a grudge or have an unresolved quarrel, ask God for forgiveness and seek peace with that person. In this way your prayer comes out sincere and unhindered.
exp.4:12:
It says that some younger widows, when they have nothing to keep them busy, fall into the habit of idleness and of going from house to house. Not only do they become idle, but they also turn into gossips, who talk too much, and busybodies, who meddle in other people's business, discussing things they should not mention.

Paul writes to Timothy, his co-worker who was overseeing the church in Ephesus, with instructions on how to care for widows. The church helped older widows who were left alone, but Paul advises not to include the younger ones on that list. His concern is that they have an orderly life and a good testimony. Some details of the previous verse are understood in different ways.

For today: unused free time without purpose can lead us into gossip. Let us look for a useful occupation, such as serving, working, or caring for others, and take care that our words build others up.
exp.2:11:
A deacon must be faithful to his wife, the husband of but one wife. He must also be a good manager of his children and of his own household.

Paul writes to Timothy, a young leader in Ephesus, to teach him how to organize the church. Earlier he speaks of overseers, and then of deacons. He asks that they first be tested, so that service is entrusted to people of good reputation. Some understand "husband of but one wife" as marital faithfulness; others debate whether it excludes the divorced. The phrase allows several interpretations.

For today: whoever serves in the church starts at home. Give time to your family, be faithful, and care for how you treat one another at home, because that is where the character is formed that later shows in service.
exp.2:10:
The passage says that the women too must have good character. "Dignified" means worthy of respect, serious, and of clean conduct. The ones who speak badly of others should not be gossips or slanderers. "Temperate" means balanced, with self-control. "Faithful in all things" speaks of people who can be trusted with everything entrusted to them.

Paul writes to Timothy to teach him how to organize the church in Ephesus. He speaks of the deacons and their requirements. The word "women" can refer to the wives of the deacons or to women who served as deaconesses. Scholars understand it in both ways, and the text does not fully settle the question.

For today: watch your words. Before you comment on something about another person, ask yourself whether it is true, whether it helps, and whether you would say it in front of them.
exp.2:1:
This verse lists the qualities a church overseer should have, the person entrusted with caring for and leading a local church. "Above reproach" means that no one can rightly bring a serious charge against him. "The husband of but one wife" is understood in several ways: faithfulness in marriage, or not having more than one wife; scholars do not fully agree. "Temperate" and "self-controlled" describe a person who governs his desires and habits. "Respectable" describes one whose conduct is orderly and honorable. "Hospitable" describes one who opens his home to others. "Able to teach" describes one who can explain the Word.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, who was serving in Ephesus. He wants the church to have leaders of proven character, so that the gospel will be well taught and well represented before everyone.

For today: before seeking a place of service, take care of your character. Strive to be someone trustworthy at home, kind to others, and willing to learn the Bible so that you can share it with humility.
exp.1:6:
He states that he speaks the truth and does not lie. He teaches "faithful and true," that is, with loyalty to God and with an authentic message.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker who was looking after the church in Ephesus. He has just spoken of Christ giving himself for everyone, and for that reason he stresses that his calling reaches people of every nation. His insistence that he is telling the truth probably strengthens his authority over those who were teaching different things, although the text gives no further details.

For today: if God has given you a task of teaching or advising others, do it with honesty and faithfulness. Speak the truth, without exaggerating or manipulating, and remember that the message of Christ is for everyone.

sum.1: Paul asks that prayers be offered for everyone, including those in authority, because God wants all people to be saved and Jesus Christ is the only mediator, the one who gave himself as a ransom. He then gives instructions for worship: men are to pray without anger, and women are to live with modesty and good works. He also places limits on women's role in teaching, a passage that is interpreted in several different ways.
sum.0: Paul is writing to Timothy, who is in Ephesus, and asks him to correct those who teach false doctrines and get caught up in endless arguments. Paul gives thanks because God showed mercy to him, even though he was a great sinner, since Christ came into the world to save sinners. He encourages Timothy to hold on to faith and a good conscience.
sum.3: Paul warns Timothy that in the latter times some will abandon the faith and follow false teachings, such as forbidding marriage or certain foods, although everything God created is good when received with thanksgiving. He asks Timothy to train himself in godliness, to be an example despite his youth, and to take care of his own life and his teaching.
sum.4: Paul teaches Timothy to treat every person in the church with respect, as if they were family, and to care for widows who are truly in need, since the family should look after its own first. He also asks that elders who lead well be honored, that accusations be handled fairly, and that Timothy keep himself pure.
sum.5: Paul teaches Timothy to honor those in authority and to reject those who teach false things out of ambition. He warns that the love of money brings many evils, and that godliness with contentment is great gain. He encourages Timothy to fight the good fight of the faith, and he asks the rich to be generous and to trust in God.
sum.2: Paul explains to Timothy what overseers and deacons should be like: people of integrity, self-controlled, faithful in their homes and with a good reputation, who serve with a clear conscience. He says that the church is the pillar and foundation of the truth, and he closes with a hymn about the great mystery of Christ, revealed in the flesh and received in glory.
